questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I know that the physics departments in Germany are good, which led me to look at Heidelberg. Later, I discovered that there were courses in Neutrino Physics which I was really interested in taking, especially since the structure was nothing like the course structure at my home university. I spoke to a professor who turned out to have worked at an institute closely related to the university, and she encouraged me to go down and reach out to this institute, and it just so happened that a few of the professors associated with the course I was looking forward to were dual hired between the university and the institute. Going to Germany has always been a dream - there is something very different about going away from tiny Denmark, and just seeing how huge everything is down here and the possibilities that allows for, has changed something in my way of thinking about what a university has the possibility of being.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: One thing that was slightly has to adjust to was the change in examination - Normally at my home university I do quite well, but down here I was afraid I would not pass the courses - not because of difficulty, but they relied more on memorization and not having access to any of the material used dutring the course. This I struggled with in the last few few, and I know all of my fellow Scandinavian Erasmus students struggled with as well. Not sure what can be done about that, but it was a major headache the last couple of weeks.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: I seemed to have struggled with it - I did not have access to any of the university when I arrived and showed up to get some university identification and found out I had missed my first lecture. I then spent the first week trying to figure out what courses to take, because the ones I had picked apparently where overlapping a lot - So the first week was stressful and I did not have the information on my email, as it only came to the Heidelberg University email.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: I received assistance from the university about how to access the online portal of the university - however, it was other students who told me where to find all this information.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing on my own

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I found housing through family connections, quite far from the city where the university is located.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: Atleast from where I lived, the commute was quite long. I live 8 km from the nearest train station, and 20 km from the university campus. Hence I biked to and fro, which meant I was very reliant on my bike for everyday living. If you do choose to live off campus, atleast live near the train station - even though the station may be 17 km away, the commute still only takes 10 minutes. So it can be fruitful to live far away, if near a station.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very far down the list for student housing, which was reduced by a lot for some reason - whereas I have been told that most people can find accomodation through the Erasmus program. So that was a bit disappointing.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was told to register 3 different ways - it changes from faculty to faculty and from course to course. very confusing. It was also unclear whether you could sign up to any course you wanted and then just not show up - which we are not allowed to at UCPH.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: First you register online with a code, to get a University account (and if you forget your code, you physically have to go to the it department). For physics, you can then register for courses on the LSF site for Heidelberg, although some professors want you to sign up in Moodle. However to find out what the course is about, you need to go on to Üebungen, which you only have access to as a student.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The IT-department, and then I contacted the Erasmus department because I did not know who else to contact, but they did not get back fro several weeks.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: unsuccessful in regards to my original choices, because there was no way of knowing the schedule until April - and I only found out late in April, as I did not have a University account.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Write very far in advance to try to figure out if they already know that courses will be overlapping - and make sure you have a back up.  I relied on my fellow students, which I should not have to - but I did not have information about who to contact.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Very satisfied - although some course structures took some getting used to. The academic level is quite high (for the appropriate courses atleast)

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer:
The courses relied much more on the individual professor than at UCPH. The professors generally did not follow books, but rather their own set of lecture notes. This was quite frustrating when you are used to following a book, but has its own merits. For one, the courses could take any shape the professor wanted, and so the students might shape the direction of the course. However, the downside was (for hand-written notes atleast) that missing any lectures was kind of bad, as the professors are not all great at writing lecture material - whereas someone who makes a best-seller physics book might have presented the material in a better way, which could then be presented by a professor (as I am used to at UCPH). 

The physics level was good - the department is much larger than at UCPH, so there are many very clever people, which was catered to by the professors. Failing a course seems much more likely down here than at UCPH. Many of the full-time students I became friends with were failing their classes, but were quite intelligent. Maybe the structure is just different, or they want to create a higher threshhold.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The are many more course structures available than at UCPH SCIENCE. There are courses from 2 ECTS to 24 ECTS. in the 2-4 ECTS range the format was very rote teaching, a lecturer lecturing to a class of students falling asleep - if they turn up.  From there on it gets better. 6 ECTS was a good format - it provided different types of courses which were challenging. For example I had a course which was quite standard in structure (lecture, lecture notes, problem sessions) yet you had time to go in depth with anything you found interesting during the lecture/problem sessions, because it was not as tight a schedule as others. Another 6 ECTS format was the seminar: Here the students of the class each pick a topic from a list/find a new topic to present to the other students, followed by a discussion, in which a few professors might jump in (4 were present for the seminar I had) - the overall topic is also stated, so people know what they are getting in to. Then there were 8 ECTS courses - these were much more akin to the lectures at UCPH SCIENCE. Very fast paced, big classrooms, not a lot of time to go in-depth, but you learn a lot.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Nonlinear Dynamics and Pattern Formation
Condensed Matter Theory 2
Standard Model of Particle Physics
Looking for the Invisible: Dark Matter and Neutrinos
Modern Aspects of Nuclear Physics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer:
The Looking for the Invisible: Dark Matter and Neutrinos seminar was very good - it allowed for a lot of questions which could be asked and fruitful discussions. 
The Condensed Matter Theory 2 Course was also good, but very fast paced if you have not read before the lectures.
The Nonlinear Dynamics and Pattern formation was very interesting, but the lecturer would trail of while writing - so very hard to follow along during the lecture, and his lecture notes were not very readable. The topic itself was quite interesting, and he was very open to questions - so a good course if you ask a lot of questions.

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I was abroad quite a bit and had some trouble coming back to Germany, so a few thousands went with that.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer:
I mostly bought food - the food was slightly cheaper than in Denmark (Copenhagen), but different things cost quite different. I was also not used to cheap cafeteria food - nobody brings a packed lunch down here. Also, going to a Café is much cheaper and good for studying. 

I also took advantage of their university library, where you can borrow any book for 3 months. So I didnt need to buy any books - which I did not need anyway, because most of the material was covered in the lecture notes, but these were awful, so I needed supplementary material.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: There are a lot of sports opportunities and the Erasmus Network hosted a lot of events for going around Germany or hiking - sadly I did not participate myself in the Erasmus Network, and I was late for the sports union and felt I got enough exercise biking back and forth from my little town.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Theater is free for students - but in German most likely. There were many reduced prices for students, including the local movie theater, which shows non-dubbed international films on specific week days.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: The movie theater was very good - very much an old school vibe. From all of my friends I also gather that the sport union is very, very good!

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Go to Königstuhl and just around the Rhine valley on a bike - or into the hills if you dare (hint: they are bigger than any hills we have in Denmark, so bring good lungs). There is good transportation opportunities to go to the big Southern and Western German cities such as Frankfurt, Stuttgart and Freiburg - all very beautiful!

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Quite easy, the Germans are not that different from the Danes - although the Church bells ringing every 15 minutes takes some getting used to. Them not being very different from the Danes also means they do not go out of their way to speak to strangers - although it is a University town, so if you speak english somebody might notice and ask where you're from. Also, nearly any young person here studies, so that's an easy in.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Get into the buddy programme! The Germans I got closest to down here (apart from my host family) were through the buddy programme.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Nothing in particular, except the language barrier at times. Oh and tipping. I hate tipping. Just include it in a fair wage.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: Although they are not very different, their history is quite different. The relationship of our generation with older generations is therefore not the same as ours. A lot of people also just have a different drive from what I have experienced in Denmark, academically and non-academically - that I found very inspiring. Being down in the South also meant people were friendlier than in Denmark, especially if you flashed them a smile. If you are not in Heidelberg however, you might have some difficulty if you do not speka any German.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Take advantage of the different structure and try to unfold your creativity - since your grades do not matter it also does not hurt to 1. Ask stupid questions and get lost in course material that does not matter much for the exam, and 2. take time out of university to explore the town and definitely join the sports union! Being a university town, I highly recommend living in the actual city - it is much easier to just pop down and meet your friends, getting to class and also getting home after a night out.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer:
Remember to take time outside of University. 

At least for Physics there is the Max Planck Institute for Nuclear Physics - reach out to them and ask about any projects - they very much encourage engagement and they do a lot of very high-end work!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Probably feeling stupid and asking stupid questions. It was very rewarding to let myself dumb down - I feel much more ready to tackle actual research now. The friends I made down here also made for a lot of fun and I look forward to seeing them again in the future!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: Balancing all of the things you want to do while on exchange - meeting new people, studying, seeing the country, practising the language, trying new things - I only managed by choosing a subset of things which I would focus on during my actual study time at the university. Maybe it works better for some to try many different things, but spending 10 hours a week on transport I was already quite low on effective time I had for exchange things.

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: Thank you for the opportunity!

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
